name: Myrtle Green
lede: Myrtle Green is a dark bluish green named for the leaf of the myrtle shrub, recorded in color charts since Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature.

sections.title: A leaf's name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary glosses myrtle green as a green resembling the green of the myrtle leaf, and notes that it is sometimes shortened to plain "myrtle", a word that has also been seen as a purple [1][2]. The dictionary files it among the greens, beside such neighbors as [[moss-green]] and [[light-green]] [2].

The Pigment Compendium has a separate, trade-side entry [3]. It lists "myrtle green" as a synonym or variant name for chrome green, on the authority of Mayer (1991) [3]. That is a pigment-maker's label, and nothing in the book says the paint matched the swatch shown here.

sections.title: On the charts
sections.body:
The name is older than the screen color. Ridgway carried it into his 1886 nomenclature, and our library traces its earliest record there [4]. In Ridgway's 1912 plates it is plate VII, hue 41, and the scanned plate reads as a darker, deeper green than the swatch on this page [4]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places the swatch in block 151, "moderate bluish green", only 1.1 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [4].

So the name has always meant a blue-leaning dark green, but the exact depth moves from chart to chart. Treat it as a family name for [[bluish-green]] darks rather than one fixed shade.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 46 works, or 0.19 per cent, which is rarer than 61 per cent of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 0.3 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century (5 paintings) [5]. It is most over-represented in French paintings, at 3.0 times the expected rate (12 of 3,443) [5]. Where it appears it usually plays a mid-tone [5].

The earliest match is a Bellini of about 1490 [5]. That is 396 years before the name's first record, so it shows a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a pigment or a dye [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [5].
